candidates.statement: The authors state that agent frameworks generally provide interfaces through which agents act on the world, environments in which agents operate, and mechanisms for human-agent or agent-agent communication, and that agent development and evaluation have become challenging as agents tackle harder problems.

Per the authors' related-work description, existing general-purpose frameworks offer building blocks with basic runtime support (LangChain/LangGraph), limited sandboxed code interpretation (CrewAI) or stateless command execution (AutoGen), and software-engineering agents such as SWE-Agent and AutoCodeRover target one domain.

In OpenHands an agent is a function from the event history (a chronological list of past actions and observations) to a new action, and the runtime is a function from an action to an observation; the state also carries accumulated LLM cost and delegation metadata.

Agents act through three primitive actions (run Python in IPython, run a bash command, interact with a browser via the BrowserGym language) executed in a per-session docker sandbox through a REST action execution API that fronts a bash shell, an IPython server and a Playwright-based Chromium browser.
The runtime can be built on an arbitrary user-provided docker image by installing the action execution API into it, and reuses images through a hash-based tag plus a generic tag.
AgentSkills is a Python library of tools auto-imported into the IPython environment; a skill is added only when the LLM cannot readily write the code itself and/or the skill calls an external model.
An agent can hand a subtask to another agent through AgentDelegateAction; the generalist CodeActAgent delegates web browsing to BrowsingAgent.
AgentHub hosts community-contributed agents: CodeActAgent (default generalist), Browsing Agent, GPTSwarm Agent and micro agents; the authors state the hub has over 10 implemented agents.
The evaluation framework integrates 15 benchmarks in three categories (7 software, 2 web, 6 miscellaneous assistance).
The authors report 32K GitHub stars, more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors, and an MIT license.

CodeActAgent v1.8 resolved 26.0% of SWE-Bench Lite (300 instances, no hint text) with claude-3-5-sonnet@20240620, 22.0% with gpt-4o-2024-05-13 and 7.0% with gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, at an average cost per instance of 1.10, 1.72 and 0.01 (USD).

On SWE-Bench Lite the 26.0% figure lies 0.3 to 1.3 points below Aider (26.3), Moatless Tools (26.7) and Agentless (27.3) and 7.0 to 8.0 points above SWE-Agent (18.0) and AutoCodeRover (19.0); the authors call this competitive with other open-source software-engineering specialists.
On HumanEvalFix (Python, 164 instances) CodeActAgent v1.5 with gpt-4o fixed 79.3% of bugs 0-shot, versus 48.6% for StarCoder2-15B and 87.7% for SWE-agent with a 1-shot demonstration.

On WebArena (812 tasks) BrowsingAgent v1.0 succeeded on 8.5% (gpt-4o-mini), 14.8% (gpt-4o) and 15.5% (claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620); CodeActAgent v1.8 delegating to BrowsingAgent scored 8.3, 14.5 and 15.3; listed comparators range from Lemur 5.3 to Auto Eval & Refine 20.2, and the WebArena baseline agent scored 14.4 with gpt-4-turbo.

On MiniWoB++ (125 environments, full set) BrowsingAgent scored 27.2% (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125) and 40.8% (gpt-4o), delegation from CodeActAgent 39.8%, against 34.6 for Workflow Guided Exploration and 91.1 for CC-NET, both trained specialist models.
On GAIA Level 1 validation (53 instances) the GPTSwarm agent scored 30.2% (gpt-4-0125-preview) and 32.1% (gpt-4o-2024-05-13), versus 13.2% for AutoGPT with gpt-4-turbo.

On the GPQA diamond set (198 instances) CodeActAgent v1.8 with claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 reached 52.0%; Table 7 lists CodeActAgent v1.5 with gpt-4o at 53.1, 49.3 and 52.8 on the diamond, main and extended subsets, against 38.8 for few-shot chain-of-thought GPT-4 on diamond and 81.3 (Table 6; 81.2 in Table 7) for expert humans.
On AgentBench OS (144 instances) CodeActAgent v1.5 with gpt-4o scored 57.6% versus 42.4% for the gpt-4 baseline agent; on MINT math (225) 77.3% versus 65.8%; on MINT code (136) 50.0% versus 59.6%.

On ProofWriter (600 five-hop instances, logical forms from Logic-LM) CodeActAgent v1.5 with gpt-4o scored 78.8% versus 79.6% for Logic-LM with gpt4 and a symbolic solver; on Entity Deduction Arena (200 instances) 38.0% versus 40.0% for zero-shot gpt-4-0314.

In the tables the best OpenHands configuration sits below the best listed comparator on eight of the ten benchmarks summarised in the article (SWE-Bench Lite, HumanEvalFix, WebArena, MiniWoB++, MINT code, ProofWriter, Entity Deduction Arena, and GPQA if expert humans are counted) and above it on GAIA, AgentBench OS and MINT math; with gpt-3.5-turbo variants OpenHands scores 11.8 vs 32.6 on AgentBench OS and 24.0 vs 27.0 on Entity Deduction Arena against gpt-3.5 baselines.

The authors interpret the results as showing that the same CodeAct agent, without changes to its system prompt, is competitive across software, web and miscellaneous tasks; the tables list different agents and versions per benchmark (CodeActAgent v1.5 and v1.8, BrowsingAgent, GPTSwarm), and comparators are often task-specialised.

The authors envision OpenHands as a catalyst for research and applications and state that it accelerates research innovations; the paper contains no measurement of such acceleration beyond the adoption statistics.

OpenHands includes integration tests that mock LLM calls with stored prompt-response pairs and compare outcomes with gold files, run on every pull request and main-branch commit across several platforms and sandbox types.

The authors list open limitations: agents still struggle with complex tasks, suffer when editing long files, and OpenHands's workflow still needs substantial handcrafted work; planned directions are principled multi-modality, integrating Auto Eval & Refine into the browsing agent, and graph-based automatic workflow generation.

The authors' ethics statement says OpenHands can help mitigate agent risks by enabling systematic evaluation, facilitating human-agent interaction rather than unsupervised autonomy, and giving researchers access to agents for safety research.

The project's later repositories, per their READMEs, extend the platform: a benchmarks repository migrating to an Agent SDK with Docker and remote workspaces, and Agent Canvas, a self-hosted control center whose frontend connects to one or more Agent Servers (REST) and can also run third-party agents through the Agent-Client Protocol.

The authors describe five components as the platform's contribution: an event-stream interaction mechanism, a docker-sandboxed runtime with bash, browser and IPython, an agent interface for creating and editing software, executing code and browsing, multi-agent delegation, and an evaluation framework.
